issues: Content sound. NG128 states last known to be well (incl. wake-up strokes) in thrombectomy recs 1.4.5-1.4.7; citation made specific (NG128 amended since 2022).

edits.why_correct: Eligibility for thrombolysis and thrombectomy depends on how long ago the stroke started. When onset was not witnessed, as with a wake-up stroke, the clock starts from the time the person was last known to be well, and treatment decisions are then guided by that time and by imaging. Source: NICE NG128, Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s, recommendations 1.4.5-1.4.7 (last known to be well, including wake-up strokes).

Clinical content correct. NICE CKS has no myasthenia gravis topic (could not verify); citation replaced. No live non-ocular generalised MG recognition item (NEU022/BX070/PAQ16007/NEU055 ocular).

edits.why_correct: Weakness that builds with repeated or sustained activity, including bulbar fatigue, and recovers with rest is the hallmark of myasthenia gravis, an antibody-mediated disorder of the neuromuscular junction. Reflexes and sensation are typically preserved and creatine kinase is normal. Diagnosis is supported by acetylcholine receptor antibodies, with further tests if these are negative. Source: Association of British Neurologists, UK guidance on the management of myasthenia gravis; NHS, Myasthenia gravis.

issues: Verified against NG71 recs 1.5.13-1.5.20 (evaluate and treat triggers; do not treat if well tolerated; reduce triggering drugs with specialist advice; quetiapine/clozapine; no olanzapine; other antipsychotics worsen motor features). Citation year simplified to the 2017 recommendations.

edits.why_correct: NICE advises a general medical evaluation for anyone with Parkinson's hallucinations and treatment of any trigger found, such as infection. If the hallucinations are well tolerated by the patient and family, they should not be treated. Treatment is considered only if they become distressing, and then involves specialist-guided dose reduction and quetiapine or clozapine. Source: NICE NG71, Parkinson's disease in adults, recommendations 1.5.13-1.5.20.

issues: Diagnosis sound. CKS page unverifiable (403) so the 2024 date was unsupported; removed. Near live PAQ14929/PAN7492/NEU010 but those are migraine with aura or a feature question; accepted.

edits.why_correct: Recurrent unilateral throbbing headaches lasting hours, with nausea and sensitivity to light, and complete recovery between attacks, fit migraine without aura. The normal examination and absence of red flags make a secondary cause unlikely. Source: NICE CKS, Migraine; NICE CG150, Headaches in over 12s.

issues: Verified NG127 1.7.2 and 1.10.2 (immediate referral for rapidly progressive symmetrical weakness/numbness; assess bulbar and respiratory function). Distinct from live NEU003/NEU102/NEU051 (inpatient management) and BX426 (diagnosis).
Anatomy correct, but NG232 does not mention anosmia; citation overstated. Replaced.

edits.why_correct: Anosmia after head trauma is typically caused by shearing of the delicate olfactory nerve fibres as they pass through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone, and it can occur even when CT is normal. Taste seems reduced because flavour depends heavily on smell, so a bland taste with normal facial and visual function points to olfactory nerve injury. Source: standard clinical neuroanatomy (olfactory nerve, cranial nerve I) and head injury teaching.

issues: Dystonia/cervical dystonia with sensory trick is correct; distractor definitions accurate. No live duplicate (NEU079/P072 are acute drug dystonia treatment).
Clinically correct (L3-L4 quadriceps, knee jerk). Citation mislabelled MRC scale (grades power, not root levels). Learning point adjacent to live BX643 (femoral nerve) but tests root level; accepted.

edits.why_correct: Straightening the knee depends on the quadriceps, which is supplied by the femoral nerve from the L3 and L4 roots, and the knee jerk is mediated by the same roots. Weak knee extension with a reduced knee jerk and normal ankle findings therefore localises to L3-L4. Source: standard myotome and reflex levels, UK undergraduate clinical neurology teaching.

issues: Todd paresis correct. NG217 does not mention Todd paresis (writer admitted); citation replaced.

edits.why_correct: Temporary focal weakness lasting minutes to hours after a seizure is Todd's paresis (postictal paralysis), thought to reflect neuronal exhaustion in the area that seized. It resolves spontaneously, and a normal scan with a clear temporal relationship to a witnessed seizure supports it. Source: standard clinical neurology teaching on postictal (Todd) paresis; Epilepsy Society.

issues: Content correct. CKS MS page unverifiable (403) so the claim of CKS review date is unsupported; citation made general. No live Lhermitte item.

edits.why_correct: Lhermitte sign is a brief electric-shock sensation running down the spine and limbs on neck flexion. It reflects irritability of demyelinated dorsal column pathways in the cervical cord and is classically described in multiple sclerosis, which fits her earlier optic neuritis. It can also occur with other cervical cord disease. Source: standard clinical neurology teaching; MS Trust, Lhermitte sign.

issues: Wernicke localisation correct; RCP stroke guideline does not give the localisation, citation overstated. Replaced. Not a duplicate of BX169 (type) or PAQ15259 (Broca location).

edits.why_correct: Fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension is receptive (Wernicke) aphasia. Wernicke area lies in the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus of the language-dominant hemisphere, which is the left in almost all right-handed people. Because the motor cortex is spared, limb strength is often normal. Source: standard clinical neuroanatomy of language areas.
